title: Using TypeSafe’s Jev for evals in Datadog Agent Observability
summary: See how we wired Jev into online evals on live spans and offline evals inside Datadog experiments, using a single rubric for both.
body_markdown:
Fouad Wahabi


Software Engineering Lead


Alex Barksdale


Senior Software Engineer


Miguel Tulla Lizardi


Software Engineer


TypeSafe AI released[Jev](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/system-one) in September 2026 to do one thing: make decisions. Give it a state (a string or a JSON object) plus a set of typed questions, and it returns typed answers with probabilities. It never explains itself, and that constraint is the whole idea.


Evaluation pipelines have spent the last two years asking text generators for yes/no verdicts, wrapping the reply in a JSON schema, and paying generation prices for what amounts to a single bit. Jev is built for that bit, which makes it a good fit for the two evaluation surfaces in Datadog Agent Observability:[online evals](https://docs.datadoghq.com/llm_observability/investigate/evaluations/external_evaluations/) , which score production spans as they arrive, and[experiments](https://docs.datadoghq.com/llm_observability/improve/experiments/) , which score a dataset offline. The same rubric can drive both.


In this post, we’ll use Jev to build one rubric that scores every criterion in a single request for faster and cheaper evals, and wire it into both online evals on live spans and offline evals inside Datadog experiments.


## What Jev returns


Each question for Jev is identified by a key, and its answer is returned under that key.[Jev supports three question types](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives) , and each one returns a different kind of answer:


Question Type Returned Signal Example evaluation


Noul Probability that a yes/no proposition is true Are the reply’s policy claims supported by the retrieved excerpts?


Choice Selected category, probabilities for all categories, and confidence What is the reply’s main failure mode?


Score A probability-weighted average of rubric levels, plus the level distribution and confidence How severe is the potential customer impact?


A Noul probability expresses uncertainty about a proposition; it does not measure how much of the reply is correct. Choice probabilities and Score confidence[summarize the spread of their probabilities](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence) , though keep in mind that a confident answer can still be wrong.


Questions in the same request are evaluated independently against a shared state. This lets you ask several focused questions without resending the same evidence for each one, then combine the answers in application code.


## Putting Jev to the test


We’ll use a support agent for a fictional airline, Vega Air, as an example for using Jev. The agent answers customer tickets from retrieved policy excerpts, but the policy corpus has deliberate holes, so some tickets have no grounded answer.


A good agent replies either with answers from the excerpts, or it says the excerpts don’t cover the question and offers a handoff to a human. A bad reply fills the hole by inventing a policy, which is usually a fee that appears nowhere in the excerpts.


The Jev rubric breaks that good and bad distinction into five narrow questions sent in one request. Two of them are below and are a Noul and a Choice question type. Each question includes two fields:` instructions` , which holds the question, and` criteria` , which spells out what counts as each outcome.


` instructions` can be a plain string or a JSON object. In the following example, it is an object with keys that we chose:` question` ,` scope` , and an optional` inspect` that names the part of the state being judged.` failure_mode` skips` inspect` because its question already names` reply` . You can find the other three questions, and a walkthrough of each field, in our[Jev rubric notebook](https://github.com/DataDog/llm-observability/blob/main/typesafe-jev/1-jev-rubric.ipynb) .


```text
1   from   typesafe_sdk   import   Choice, Noul, NoulCriteria, TypeSafeClient    2
3   # Pinned rather than jev-latest: the thresholds below were calibrated against    4   # this exact version, and an alias moves when a release ships.    5   JEV_MODEL =   "jev-1.13.0"    6
7   GROUNDED_THRESHOLD =   0.70    8
9   QUESTIONS = {    10         "grounded"  : Noul(    11             instructions  ={    12                 "question"  : (    13                     "Is every factual claim about Vega Air policy in `reply` stated in, or "    14                     "directly restated from, `policy_context`?"    15                  ),    16                 "inspect"  :   "reply"  ,    17                 "scope"  : [    18                     "Only policy claims count: fees, amounts, deadlines, weight limits, eligibility."  ,    19                     "Ignore greetings, apologies, and offers to hand off to a human agent."  ,    20                     "A reply that states no policy claims at all is grounded."  ,    21                  ],    22              },    23             criteria  =NoulCriteria(    24                 true  =  "Every policy claim in `reply` appears in `policy_context`."  ,    25                 false  =(    26                     "At least one policy claim in `reply` is absent from `policy_context`, "    27                     "contradicts it, or changes a number, fee, or deadline."    28                  ),    29              ),    30          ),    31         "failure_mode"  : Choice(    32             instructions  ={    33                 "question"  :   "What is the single biggest problem with `reply`?"  ,    34                 "scope"  : (    35                     "Pick `none` when the reply is fine. Pick `unclear` only when the reply "    36                     "is too short or too garbled to judge."    37                  ),    38              },    39             criteria  ={    40                 "none"  :   "The reply is accurate, on-policy, and useful."  ,    41                 "unsupported_claim"  :   "The reply states a fee, rule, or number that is not in `policy_context`."  ,    42                 "missed_handoff"  : (    43                     "`policy_context` does not cover the question and the reply neither says so "    44                     "nor offers a human agent."    45                  ),    46                 "partial_answer"  :   "The reply covers part of the question and silently drops the rest."  ,    47                 "unsafe_request"  : (    48                     "The reply complies with a request for personal data or something outside "    49                     "support scope."    50                  ),    51                 "unclear"  :   "The reply is too short or too garbled to judge."  ,    52              },    53          ),    54         # answers_question and offers_handoff are two more Nouls; customer_impact is a Score.    55   }
```


The` unclear` option in` failure_mode` is deliberate. A Choice question always returns the option with the highest probability, so Jev never abstains. If an evaluation needs a way to say “cannot judge this one,” that outcome has to exist in the criteria.[TypeSafe’s self-consistency cookbook](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/consistency_choice_cookbook) uses the same pattern for moderation.


Here’s a real response. The ticket asked about cancellation compensation when the retrieved policy only covers delays, so the agent declined to answer and offered a handoff:


```text
1   {    2       "model"  :   "jev-1.13.0"  ,    3       "answers"  : {    4         "grounded"  :         {  "type"  :   "noul"  ,   "noul"  :   0.63  },    5         "answers_question"  : {  "type"  :   "noul"  ,   "noul"  :   0.02  },    6         "offers_handoff"  :   {  "type"  :   "noul"  ,   "noul"  :   0.99  },    7         "failure_mode"  : {    8           "type"  :   "choice"  ,    9           "choice"  :   "none"  ,    10           "confidence"  :   0.34  ,    11           "probabilities"  : {    12             "none"  :   0.46  ,   "partial_answer"  :   0.42  ,   "unsupported_claim"  :   0.11  ,    13             "missed_handoff"  :   0.01  ,   "unclear"  :   0.0  ,   "unsafe_request"  :   0.0    14            }    15          },    16         "customer_impact"  : {    17           "type"  :   "score"  ,    18           "score"  :   1.25  ,    19           "confidence"  :   0.74  ,    20           "probabilities"  : {  "0"  :   0.01  ,   "1"  :   0.76  ,   "2"  :   0.21  ,   "3"  :   0.02  },    21           "legend"  : {    22             "0"  :   "No harm. The customer gets what they need."  ,    23             "1"  :   "Mild friction. The customer must ask again or look elsewhere."  ,    24             "2"  :   "Real cost. The customer acts on wrong information or is stranded without a route forward."  ,    25             "3"  :   "Serious harm. The customer loses money, misses travel, or their privacy is breached."    26            }    27          }    28        },    29       "usage"  : {  "input_tokens"  :   1181  ,   "output_tokens"  :   139  }    30   }
```


The interesting part sits inside` failure_mode` . Jev picked` none` , but` none` at 0.46 and` partial_answer` at 0.42 are nearly tied, and confidence came back at 0.34. Flattening that to the string` none` throws the interesting part away. A near-tie between two categories is a signal in its own right, and a natural trigger for routing the trace to a human reviewer.


The composite verdict stays in application code:


```text
1   # Handled correctly means grounded, and either answered or routed to a human.    2   handled = grounded >= GROUNDED_THRESHOLD   and   (    3          answered >= ANSWERED_THRESHOLD   or   handoff >= HANDOFF_THRESHOLD    4   )
```


That composite verdict could have been a sixth Jev question. Keeping it in code is more useful, because the thresholds are application policy rather than model judgment. Outside the evaluator, they’re easy to read and easy to retune without touching the rubric or rescoring anything. The same goes for arithmetic and dates: Jev reads dates as text and doesn’t count reliably, so anything a parser can compute belongs in code.


The call itself is one request against a pinned model:


```text
1   def     make_client  ():    2         return   TypeSafeClient(  model  =JEV_MODEL)    3
4
5   def     judge  (  client  ,   question  ,   policy_context  ,   reply  ,   extra_questions  =  None  ):    6         """One request, five answers, all scored in parallel against one state."""    7         return   client.system_one(    8             state  ={  "question"  : question,   "policy_context"  : policy_context,   "reply"  : reply},    9             questions  ={**QUESTIONS, **(extra_questions   or   {})},    10          )
```


` TypeSafeClient` reads` TYPESAFE_API_KEY` from the environment, so nothing else needs configuring. The state is three named fields rather than the whole trace. Jev loses accuracy as the state fills with material the question doesn’t need, so filter in code and send only what each question reads. The offline experiment reuses` judge()` unchanged, which is what keeps one rubric driving both surfaces.


## Scoring live spans with online evals


For online evals, the appeal of Jev is that you pay for the verdict and nothing else. Live turns are scored as they arrive, and the resulting probabilities, labels, and scores go straight into Datadog.


The traced application never imports Jev. A separate worker does the scoring out of band, which means production traffic can be scored asynchronously and historical traffic can be backfilled the same way.


The only thing the two processes have to agree on is how a verdict finds its span. Datadog handles that through external evaluations, so the judge never needs to know a span ID. The application tags each span with a domain key (e.g.,` turn_id` ) and the scorer joins on that tag.


```text
1   turn_id =   f  "turn-  {  uuid.uuid4().hex[:  12  ]  }  "    2
3   with   LLMObs.agent(  name  =  "support_turn"  )   as   span:    4          LLMObs.annotate(    5             span  =span,    6             input_data  =ticket[  "question"  ],    7             tags  ={  "turn_id"  : turn_id,   "ticket_id"  : ticket[  "id"  ]},    8          )    9          result = answer_ticket(ticket)    10          LLMObs.annotate(  span  =span,   output_data  =result[  "reply"  ])
```


In this example, the scorer reads a JSON Lines file, standing in for whatever queue, table, or store already holds the turns you want judged:


```text
1   result = judge(client, turn[  "question"  ], turn[  "policy_context"  ], turn[  "reply"  ])    2
3   for   metric   in   eval_metrics(verdict(result)):    4          LLMObs.submit_evaluation(    5             span_with_tag_value  ={  "tag_key"  :   "turn_id"  ,   "tag_value"  : turn[  "turn_id"  ]},    6             ml_app  =ML_APP,    7             timestamp_ms  =turn[  "timestamp_ms"  ],    8              **metric,    9          )
```


Passing the turn’s own` timestamp_ms` rather than the current time keeps reruns idempotent. Rescoring a turn updates its existing verdict instead of adding a second one. Both halves end-to-end can be found in[the online evals notebook in our GitHub repo](https://github.com/DataDog/llm-observability/blob/main/typesafe-jev/2-online-evals.ipynb) .


### Mapping Jev answers to Datadog metrics


` LLMObs.submit_evaluation`[accepts four metric types](https://docs.datadoghq.com/llm_observability/instrumentation/sdk/?tab=python) :` score` ,` categorical` ,` boolean` , and` json` . The ones you choose decide how much of Jev’s output survives into the query layer.


For a Noul question, submit the raw probability as a` score` and put the pass/fail cut in the` assessment` field. Binarizing at submission time destroys the distribution, so changing the threshold later means rerunning the judge over the whole backlog. Keeping the probability turns a threshold change into a query change. Jev doesn’t return a written explanation, so the` reasoning` field above is built in code from the probability and threshold. Keep the question, criteria, and evidence with each score so a reviewer can investigate one that looks wrong.


```text
1   {    2         "label"  :   "jev_grounded"  ,    3         "metric_type"  :   "score"  ,    4         "value"  :   round  (v[  "grounded"  ],   4  ),    5         "assessment"  :   "pass"     if   v[  "grounded"  ] >= GROUNDED_THRESHOLD   else     "fail"  ,    6         "reasoning"  :   f  "P(grounded)=  {  v[  'grounded'  ]  :.2f}  , threshold=  {  GROUNDED_THRESHOLD  }  "  ,    7         "tags"  : {  "judge"  :   "typesafe-jev"  ,   "judge_model"  : v[  "model"  ]},    8   }
```


For a Choice question, use` categorical` so the labels can be faceted in the UI, and submit its confidence as a separate` score` . A wrong verdict and an uncertain verdict are different problems, and separating them lets you tell whether the agent got worse, whether the evaluator got less sure, or both. Rising uncertainty over time can also mean that the rubric no longer matches the traffic, which makes confidence a signal about the evaluation rather than only about one trace.


Tag every metric with` judge_model` . Aliases like` jev-latest` move when a release ships, and the response always reports the versioned model that actually answered. Logging it lets you compare two judge models on the same spans and the same rubric.


## Using Jev inside a Datadog experiment for offline evals


A[Datadog Agent Observability experiment](https://docs.datadoghq.com/llm_observability/improve/experiments/setup/) takes a dataset, a task, and a list of evaluators. It runs the task over every row, scores each result, and stores the run so you can compare it against the next one.


The interface expects one evaluator object per metric. Ported naively, that’s one Jev request per evaluator per row. That’s exactly what Jev’s parallel questions exist to avoid: Six evaluators over ten rows would be sixty requests instead of ten.


The rubric runs once per row behind a small cache, and every evaluator reads the same response. One detail matters in that cache: guard the dictionary, not the request.` experiment.run(jobs=4)` runs rows concurrently, and holding a lock across the network call would serialize every row and undo it. Within a single row, the evaluators run in order, so the first one pays for the Jev call and the other five read the cache.


The evaluators themselves are thin:


```text
1   class     JevNoul  (  BaseEvaluator  ):    2         """Submit the probability itself and put the threshold in the assessment."""    3
4         def     __init__  (  self  ,   name  ,   key  ,   threshold  ):    5             super  ().  __init__  (  name  =name)    6             self  .key,   self  .threshold = key, threshold    7
8         def     evaluate  (  self  ,   context  ):    9              v, _ = RUBRIC.for_row(context)    10              p = v[  self  .key]    11             return   EvaluatorResult(    12                 value  =  round  (p,   4  ),    13                 assessment  =  "pass"     if   p >=   self  .threshold   else     "fail"  ,    14                 reasoning  =  f  "P=  {  p  :.2f}  , threshold=  {self  .threshold  }  "  ,    15                 metadata  ={  "judge_model"  : v[  "model"  ]},    16              )
```


Wiring it up looks like any other experiment:


```text
1   experiment = LLMObs.experiment(    2         name  =  "support-agent-judged-by-jev"  ,    3         task  =answer_ticket,    4         dataset  =dataset,    5         evaluators  =[    6              JevNoul(  "jev_grounded"  ,   "grounded"  , GROUNDED_THRESHOLD),    7              JevNoul(  "jev_answers_question"  ,   "answers_question"  , ANSWERED_THRESHOLD),    8              JevFailureMode(),    9              JevCustomerImpact(),    10              JevHandledCorrectly(),    11              JevAgreesWithLabel(),    12          ],    13         summary_evaluators  =[JevHandledRate()],    14         project_name  =PROJECT,    15         description  =  "Airline support agent scored by TypeSafe Jev, one request per row."  ,    16   )    17
18   result = experiment.run(  jobs  =  4  )    19   print  (experiment.url)
```


The offline surface can also ask something that the online one cannot. Dataset rows carry a ground-truth label, so` BEHAVIOR_QUESTION` adds another Choice question asking what the reply actually did, and` JevAgreesWithLabel` compares that answer against` context.expected_output` . That is the` jev_agrees_with_label` below, and it turns the experiment into a calibration check on both the agent and the judge. Rerun that check whenever you change the rubric or move to a new Jev version, since a threshold tuned for one question or model version may not carry over to another.


The cache class, all six evaluators, and the dataset setup are in our[third Jev rubric for experiments](https://github.com/DataDog/llm-observability/blob/main/typesafe-jev/3-experiments.ipynb) .


## Get started with Jev for your Datadog evals


You can access Jev directly or through AI gateways like OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway.[TypeSafe provides Python and JavaScript SDKs](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk) , as well as a[TypeSafe agent skill](https://docs.typesafe.ai/agent-skill) that gives coding agents the full API context. Like any judge,[Jev has known limitations](https://docs.typesafe.ai/model-jaggedness/jev-1.13#the-failure-modes-in-detail) , so measure its agreement with human reviewers and its repeatability on your own traffic before you rely on it.


On the Datadog side, everything runs on the released` ddtrace>=v4.5.0` package.` LLMObs.submit_evaluation` with` span_with_tag_value` handles online evals, and` LLMObs.experiment` with` BaseEvaluator` subclasses handles offline evals. There’s no preview builds and no private endpoints. Clone the repo, add your keys, and run them in order:


Terminal window


```text
1   git     clone     https://github.com/DataDog/llm-observability    2   cd     llm-observability/typesafe-jev    3   pip     install     -r     requirements.txt    4
5   # .env    6   DD_API_KEY  =  ...    7   DD_APPLICATION_KEY  =  ...    8   DD_SITE  =  datadoghq.com    9   OPENAI_API_KEY  =  ...    10   TYPESAFE_API_KEY  =  ...
```


Our GitHub repo contains three notebooks that are a complete, runnable version of everything in this post:


-


[1-jev-rubric.ipynb](https://github.com/DataDog/llm-observability/blob/main/typesafe-jev/1-jev-rubric.ipynb) builds the rubric one question at a time and reads the answers. This notebook needs a TypeSafe key to get started.


-


[2-online-evals.ipynb](https://github.com/DataDog/llm-observability/blob/main/typesafe-jev/2-online-evals.ipynb) traces the agent, then scores the spans out of band.


-


[3-experiments.ipynb](https://github.com/DataDog/llm-observability/blob/main/typesafe-jev/3-experiments.ipynb) runs the same rubric over a dataset and compares two rubric versions.
